title: Marginal-Fermi-Liquid-like Behavior without Pseudogap in Infinite-Layer Nickelates
authors: Yu Fan, Zhitong An, Xiang Ding, Xingtian Sun, Yutong Chen, Zhihui Chen, Shenglin Tang, Chihao Li, Jiahao Ye, Timur Kim, Haichao Xu, Rui Peng, Donglai Feng
abstract: Pseudogap formation, strange-metal behavior and unconventional superconductivity are closely intertwined in hole-doped cuprates, yet their relationship remains unresolved. Infinite-layer nickelates offer a distinct 3d9-derived platform to address this question by combining a cuprate-like Ni dx2-y2 Fermi surface with multiband electronic degrees of freedom. Here we use angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy to resolve the low-energy spectral function of superconducting La0.8Ca0.2NiO2 and parent LaNiO2 thin films. In La0.8Ca0.2NiO2, the electronic self-energy Im Sigma(omega) is approximately linear in energy and its slope increases from (pi/2, pi/2) to (pi, 0), revealing momentum-dependent marginal-Fermi-liquid-like scattering. Both films show a progressive suppression of low-energy spectral weight from the diagonal direction toward (pi, 0), with stronger suppression in parent LaNiO2. However, finite Fermi-level spectral weight persists around the entire Fermi surface, with no leading-edge shift or back-bending indicative of pseudogap formation in either the electron pocket or the cuprate-like hole band. Our results demonstrate that momentum-selective correlations and marginal-Fermi-liquid-like scattering can occur without a detectable cuprate-like pseudogap, providing a benchmark for identifying the essential normal-state electronic ingredients of high-temperature superconductivity.
summary: Using ARPES on infinite-layer nickelates, this work investigates whether pseudogap formation is necessary for unconventional superconductivity. The authors report evidence of marginal-Fermi-liquid scattering and momentum-dependent correlations in these materials while definitively showing the absence of a detectable cuprate-like pseudogap opening.
main_problem: To resolve the relationship between pseudogap formation, strange-metal behavior, and unconventional superconductivity in a system distinct from cuprates.
main_result: The study found evidence of marginal-Fermi-liquid-like scattering and momentum-dependent correlations in infinite-layer nickelates without observing a detectable cuprate-like pseudogap opening.
method: Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) was used on superconducting La0.8Ca0.2NiO2 and parent LaNiO2 thin films, supplemented by transport measurements.
model_or_system: The research focuses on infinite-layer nickelates ($	ext{La}_{1-x}	ext{Ca}_x	ext{NiO}_2$), which provide a $3d^9$-derived platform to study high-temperature superconductivity phenomenology, contrasting them with hole-doped cuprates.
key_observables: Low-energy spectral function, electronic self-energy ($	ext{Im}\Sigma(\omega)$), quasiparticle peak dispersion, and resistivity vs. temperature ($T$).
important_parameters: Hole doping level (e.g., $p \sim 0.09$), superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$), and the energy scale of the pseudogap.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed spectral weight suppression is characteristic of marginal-Fermi-liquid behavior, providing a benchmark for understanding normal-state electronic ingredients.
figures_summary: Figures detail ARPES results showing continuous band dispersion up to $E_F$ and momentum-dependent spectral weight suppression in both doped and parent nickelates, contrasting with expected pseudogap signatures.
paper_structure: The paper systematically presents ARPES data on the superconducting state ($	ext{La}_{0.8}	ext{Ca}_{0.2}	ext{NiO}_2$) to establish MFL-like scattering without a gap, followed by analysis of the parent compound ($	ext{LaNiO}_2$), and concluding with a comparison to cuprate phenomenology.
why_interesting: This work provides crucial experimental data on a different class of strongly correlated superconductors, helping refine theoretical models that attempt to unify the physics governing strange-metal behavior across various high-$T_c$ materials.
